# Speaking: nine useful sentence patterns, taught by function

**Source:** [IELTS Speaking – 9 Most Common Sentence Patterns](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo), video ID `SMCwpfJMdMo`. The auto-generated English transcript was reviewed through 13:27 of the 13:30 video. The quiz contrasts ordinary, accurate language with ornate or memorized options. This note preserves the useful functional patterns, while treating the claimed usage frequencies, score guarantees, and VIP-course outcomes as unverified.

## The nine patterns and what they do

### Part 1: answer familiar questions directly

1. **“I’m a [job].”** Give the role or study status directly. Add a short, relevant detail if it helps answer the question; a longer job-title formula does not make the answer more advanced. ([0:21–1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=21s))
2. **“I’m from [place].”** Use the ordinary place-of-origin phrase that expresses the intended meaning. The video contrasts it with grammatically possible but less natural or unnecessarily formal alternatives. ([1:10–1:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=70s))
3. **“I like…”, “I prefer…”, “I normally…”, “I live in…”** Select a pattern for the answer’s function: preference, habitual activity, or place of residence. ([1:58–2:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=118s))

### Part 2: tell the event accurately

4. **Past simple for completed events:** the quiz uses a visit to a city to show the past simple as a common way to narrate an event. It also names past continuous, past perfect, and past perfect continuous as narrative options. These are resources for expressing time relationships; the task does not reward adding a tense that the story does not need. ([2:50–3:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=170s))
5. **Match tense to meaning.** The video flags “I went to London for three years” as unsuitable for a continuing three-year residence. Teach learners to choose a verb and tense that accurately express duration, sequence, and completion. The source’s larger point is useful: a sentence must be appropriate to the message and grammatically accurate, not merely look complex. ([3:50–4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=230s))
6. **“I felt [adjective].”** When asked about a reaction, state the feeling plainly and accurately. The video contrasts this with memorized-sounding poetry and incorrect idiom use; for example, *over the moon* requires the article. Use idiomatic language only when it fits the meaning and register. ([5:24–7:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=324s))

### Part 3: state, explain, and support a view

7. **Opinion and stance phrases:** “I totally agree,” “not necessarily,” “it’s possible that…,” and “in my opinion” express different functions—agreement, disagreement or qualification, possibility, and a personal view. Choose the one that matches the position; do not memorize a starter and apply it to every question. ([7:09–9:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=429s))
8. **“Because…”** Give a reason for the position. The video emphasizes that a common word can communicate the relationship clearly; a more elaborate phrase is useful only when it is accurate and natural. ([9:16–10:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=556s))
9. **“For example…” / “On the other hand…”** Support a view with a relevant example, or develop another side of the issue where that genuinely advances the answer. The video’s quiz also catches missing articles in *on the other hand* and *in a nutshell*. A summary phrase such as *to sum up* is optional and may be unnecessary in a conversational answer. ([10:19–12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=619s))

## What the course should teach

Teach these as flexible sentence functions, not as a script: answer directly, state a view, explain it, and support or qualify it. Learners should build accurate variants through practice with many questions, then check relevance, grammar, vocabulary, and understandable pronunciation. The useful theme is “choose the language that does the job”; do not claim that using these nine patterns guarantees a band score.

The video says its patterns were found by AI analysis of thousands of Band 7–9 performances, but it provides no dataset, prompts, selection method, or examples of the analysis. Treat “most common” as the creator’s description of the patterns, not an established frequency ranking or a set of examiner-preferred phrases. Official IELTS assesses Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation; it does not award marks for using this specific phrase list. ([official IELTS Speaking criteria](https://ielts.org/take-a-test/test-types/ielts-academic-test/ielts-academic-format-speaking), [Speaking band descriptors](https://ielts.org/cdn/ielts-guides/ielts-speaking-band-descriptors.pdf))

The video also inserts a free-course offer and a paid-course discount. Its “most successful course in the world” statement and claimed outcomes are marketing claims, not evidence for the lesson’s language recommendations. ([4:59–5:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=299s), [8:35–9:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SMCwpfJMdMo&t=515s))
